title: Lambda expressions and closures (anonymous functions and capture)
hook: A lambda is a short anonymous function you write inline. If it reads a local variable or instance field, the compiler builds a closure that keeps that data alive — which can pin a whole request object longer than you expect.

blocks.text: A **lambda expression** is an anonymous function written as `(parameters) => expression` or `(parameters) => { statements; }`. The compiler converts it to a **delegate** (Action, Func, or a custom type) or, when the target is Expression<TDelegate>, to an **expression tree** for providers like Entity Framework. A **closure** is the compiler-generated class that holds captured variables when a lambda reads outer locals, parameters, or instance state.

entries.plainDefinition: An inline anonymous function that converts to a delegate or expression tree.
Compiler-generated storage for variables a lambda captures from its enclosing scope.
entries.example: var threshold = 10; nums.Where(n => n > threshold); // threshold is captured

entries.plainDefinition: A lambda marked static that cannot capture locals, parameters, or instance members. Added in C# 9.
A data structure representing code as a tree, not executable IL. Used by IQueryable providers to translate to SQL.

blocks.text: Lambdas power LINQ, Task callbacks, and event handlers. Capturing `this` — even by touching an instance field — keeps the enclosing object alive for as long as the delegate is reachable. On a high-concurrency path that caches attempt submissions, an innocent capturing lambda can pin the whole request graph until the Task completes. Use **static** lambdas on hot paths to prove no capture. C# 14 lets lambda parameters take ref/in/out/scoped modifiers without repeating types.

blocks.title: Statement lambdas cannot become expression trees
blocks.body: Only expression-bodied lambdas (a single expression, no block body) can convert to Expression<TDelegate>. A block with multiple statements always becomes a delegate.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Write the lambda
items.body: Use expression form for simple cases: x => x + 1. Use block form for multiple statements.

items.title: Compiler picks the target
items.body: If the expected type is a delegate, the compiler emits a method plus optional closure class. If the target is Expression<T>, it builds an expression tree instead.

items.title: Capture analysis
items.body: Reading outer locals or instance members triggers a display class. static forbids capture entirely.

items.title: Invoke or translate
items.body: Delegates run as IL. Expression trees are inspected by providers (EF Core, etc.) and translated to SQL or other backends.

diagram.title: Lambda to delegate or expression tree
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  L[Lambda expression] --> T{Target type?}
  T -->|Func / Action / custom delegate| D[Emit method + optional closure class]
  T -->|Expression TDelegate| E[Build expression tree]
  D --> I[Invoke at runtime]
  E --> P[Provider translates e.g. to SQL]

rows: Captures this only if you reference instance members
Arrow functions capture lexical this from enclosing scope
static lambda (C# 9) — compiler error on capture
No direct equivalent; you discipline yourself
No built-in query translation from function AST
Shared mutable captures across Task.WhenAll are data races
Same pitfall with shared let variables in async callbacks

blocks.title: Subscribing a capturing lambda to a static event
blocks.body: A static event on a long-lived host plus a capturing lambda that references this keeps the subscriber alive forever unless you -= in Dispose.

blocks.title: Expecting a statement lambda in IQueryable
blocks.body: EF Core and other IQueryable providers need expression trees. A block-bodied lambda becomes a delegate and will fail or run client-side unexpectedly.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: a closure leak shows up as gen-0 allocations and retained request objects in a dotnet-gcdump after a traffic spike — look for display class types holding HttpContext or byte[] from a capturing cache factory. Expression trees fail at runtime with 'could not be translated' when you pass a block-bodied lambda to IQueryable; inspect EF Core logs for client evaluation warnings. BenchmarkDotNet comparing static vs capturing lambdas on a hot Select path quantifies closure allocation cost.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Convenient but extends captured object lifetime

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying all lambdas become expression trees — only when the target type is Expression<TDelegate> and the body is a single expression. Not knowing closure display classes allocate and pin captured objects. Using a capturing lambda on a static event without unsubscribing and calling it a 'minor style issue'. Expecting EF to translate a block-bodied lambda with local variables.

interviewTakeaways: A lambda converts to a delegate (IL + optional closure) or to Expression<T> (AST for query providers) — never both from one syntax.
Capturing allocates a display class; static lambda is the compiler-enforced no-capture form on hot paths.
In production, EF 'client evaluation' warnings mean your lambda became a delegate, not a translatable expression tree.
60s: Lambdas target delegates or Expression<T>. Statement bodies cannot be trees. Capture = display class. static = no capture. IQueryable needs Expression<Func<...>> with expression body.
Follow-up: what does the compiler emit for a lambda that captures three locals — one display class or three?
commonPitfalls: Saying every lambda is an expression tree gets you rejected — only Expression<TDelegate> targets with expression bodies.
Subscribing a capturing lambda to a static event and never unsubscribing — pins the subscriber until process exit.
Strong answer: 'Delegate for runtime invoke. Expression tree for IQueryable translation. static on hot paths. Profile closure allocations with BenchmarkDotNet if Select runs millions of times.'

jsTsCorrelations.concept: Closures and lexical this vs arrow functions
jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript arrows capture lexical this. C# lambdas capture this only if you reference instance members; static forbids it. JavaScript has no static lambda equivalent.

TypeScript has no built-in expression-tree layer — ORMs use string builders or metadata. C# Expression<T> lets EF walk the AST at runtime and emit SQL. JS/TS arrow functions always compile to callable JS, never to a translatable query AST.
